name: Oniguruma
baseline: PCRE2 (pcre2_match interpreter; pcre2_jit_match and pcre2_dfa_match also measured); secondary baseline C++ std::regex
workload: Time to find all matches of each of 18 regexes (literals, alternations, bounded repeats, case-insensitive, Unicode) over a ~16 MB English text file (3200.txt) with the rust-leipzig/regex-performance harness, 5 repeats per test, compile time excluded; Oniguruma runs with ONIG_ENCODING_ASCII and ONIG_SYNTAX_DEFAULT.
claimed_speedup: Mixed result, numbers in ms read from the repo's results_20221012.png (shown in the README). Versus PCRE2 interpreter ('pcre' column), Oniguruma is faster on 10 of the 17 patterns it can run: [a-z]shing 9.5 vs 432.9; [a-q][^u-z]{13}x 22.8 vs 417.5; .{0,2}(Tom|Sawyer|Huckleberry|Finn) 48.8 vs 3201.7; .{2,4}(Tom|Sawyer|Huckleberry|Finn) 48.2 vs 3330.2; \s[a-zA-Z]{0,12}ing\s 42.2 vs 314.9; ([A-Za-z]awyer|[A-Za-z]inn)\s 114.6 vs 755.5; [a-zA-Z]+ing 379.9 vs 837.3 (ratios 45.6x, 18.3x, 65.6x, 69.1x, 7.5x, 6.6x, 2.2x, derived from page data). Versus PCRE2 JIT ('pcre-jit' column) it wins on only 4 of 17: [a-q][^u-z]{13}x 22.8 vs 114.8 (5.0x); .{0,2}(Tom|...) 48.8 vs 176.3 (3.6x); .{2,4}(Tom|...) 48.2 vs 166.7 (3.5x); \s[a-zA-Z]{0,12}ing\s 42.2 vs 59.7 (1.4x) (derived from page data). It is slower than the interpreter on 7 patterns, for example Twain 11.2 vs 2.5, ∞|✓ 21.1 vs 0.5 and (.*?,){13}z 5558.3 vs 567.5 (JIT 32.6). Versus std::regex ('cppstd' column) it is faster on all 15 patterns where both ran, e.g. [a-q][^u-z]{13}x 22.8 vs 726.3 and .{0,2}(Tom|...) 48.8 vs 1941.8.
compiler_and_flags: Harness CMake default build type Release: -O3 with -march=native (C11/C++11, GCC-style warning flags such as -Wstack-usage); compiler name and version not stated. Oniguruma, PCRE2 (PCRE2_SUPPORT_JIT=ON) and the other engines are built by the harness from upstream master in Release mode (vendor/CMakeLists.txt), versions unpinned.
hardware: AMD Threadripper 3960X (Zen2) at 3.8 GHz, Ubuntu 20.04.5 LTS
stars_or_usage: 2.5k stars (repo archived read-only 2025-04-24; benchmark repo rust-leipzig/regex-performance 124 stars, Apache-2.0)
tradeoffs: Backtracking matcher, so pathological patterns blow up (the (.*?,){13}z row takes 5558.3 ms against 32.6 ms for PCRE2 JIT and 21.1 ms for RE2). Ruby/Oniguruma syntax and many per-regex character encodings rather than Perl/PCRE syntax and Unicode properties (the \p{Sm} row is n/a for it). No JIT. Project ended and archived by the author on 2025-04-24, so it is now a frozen codebase.
caveats: Third-party community shootout, not a project claim: Oniguruma's own README and docs carry no benchmark. The numbers exist only as a PNG (results_20221012.png, October 2022 run), not as a data file, and were read from the image. The README says the tool prints the best time of 5 repeats but src/onig.c and pcre2.c fill a times array and report mean and standard deviation. Compiler is not named, tier A is therefore borderline; Oniguruma and PCRE2 versions are whatever master was in 2022. Match counts are printed but not asserted equal across engines, and Oniguruma runs in ASCII encoding while PCRE2 runs in default (non-UTF) mode with PCRE2_MULTILINE, so semantics are close but not identical. It loses to PCRE2 JIT on 13 of 17 patterns, so the win holds only against the interpreter, not against the usual fast PCRE2 configuration. Snippet-only, not opened (hosts blocked here): a 2003 mailing-list post by the author said Oniguruma was 10-20% faster than PCRE 3.9 under ASCII encoding (obsolete PCRE 3.x), and Heng Li's regex benchmark (onig-posix 5.9.2 vs PCRE 8.10 and RE2 2010) was summarised as onig fastest on '|'-free regexes; neither used PCRE2.
found_via: seed-list mining backfill: curated lists https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp#Regular Expression and https://github.com/oz123/awesome-c#Regex (listing of https://github.com/kkos/oniguruma); numbers found via WebSearch 'Oniguruma vs PCRE2 benchmark performance regex library comparison' and the shootout README https://github.com/rust-leipzig/regex-performance
